hints: Look at lactic acid $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ and spot the two groups that can react together, the $\text{-OH}$ on one molecule and the $\text{-COOH}$ on the next.
Think about what small molecule is lost when $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-COOH}$ join, and what linkage is left joining the residues in the chain.
walkthrough:
See how one molecule can join to itself**
Lactic acid is special because it has both an alcohol $\text{-OH}$ and a carboxylic acid $\text{-COOH}$ in the same molecule. Imagine the $\text{-OH}$ of one molecule reacting with the $\text{-COOH}$ of the next. Water $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is eliminated and an ester $\text{-COO-}$ bridge is left.

Build two residues with open ends**
Draw $\text{-O-CH(-CH}_3\text{)-C(=O)-}$ then immediately $\text{-O-CH(-CH}_3\text{)-C(=O)-}$ again. Show every $\text{C-O}$, $\text{C-C}$, $\text{C=O}$ and $\text{C-H}$ bond as a line, you may write $\text{-CH}_3$ as a group. Put a trailing bond through the left hand O and the right hand C=O to show the chain continues.

Mark the repeat unit**
Bracket one $\text{-O-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-}$ section and label it repeat unit. That is the lactic acid residue minus $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, formula $\text{C}_3\text{H}_4\text{O}_2$ as a repeating block.

Final answer: Structure shows $\text{-O-CH(CH}_3\text{)-C(=O)-O-CH(CH}_3\text{)-C(=O)-}$ with continuation bonds at both ends, all bonds fully displayed except $\text{-CH}_3$, containing at least two monomer residues joined by ester linkages. One $\text{-O-CH(CH}_3\text{)-CO-}$ unit labelled as repeat unit.

hints: Recall the two main polymerisation types, addition with C=C opening versus one that ejects a small molecule like water at each join.
walkthrough:
Link water loss to the name**
Each new bond between monomers throws out $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: $$\text{-OH + HOOC-} \rightarrow \text{-OOC- + H}_2\text{O}$$ Any polymerisation that ejects a small molecule at each step is condensation. The $\text{-COO-}$ link formed from alcohol plus acid is always an ester.

Final answer: type of polymerisation: condensation
functional group: ester

hints: Think about whether the ester links in PLA can be broken by water in the environment, the reverse of how they formed.
walkthrough:
Reverse the formation reaction**
Ester bonds are easily attacked by water: $$\text{-COO- + H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{-COOH + HO-}$$ In soil or compost, water and enzymes hydrolyse the PLA chain back to lactic acid units which microbes can digest, so the plastic does not persist.
Final answer: Yes, readily biodegradable because the ester linkages can be hydrolysed by water / enzymes to give back small molecules.

hints: Match each proton type in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ to Table 8.1, note that $\text{-COOH}$ is very deshielded near $\delta$ 9 to 13 and $\text{-CH}_3$ next to CH is near $\delta$ 1 to 2.
Read the $\delta$ values directly off the Fig. 8.1 x-axis for the four sample peaks, ignoring the tiny peak at $\delta$ 0.0.
Apply the n+1 rule by counting equivalent protons on the adjacent carbon, remembering $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-COOH}$ protons do not normally split or cause splitting.
walkthrough:
Assign the shifts from the spectrum and table**
The far downfield singlet at $\delta$ 12 is classic $\text{RCOOH}$ ($\delta$ 9.0 to 13.0). The doublet at $\delta$ 1.6 is alkane $\text{-CH}_3$ ($\delta$ 0.9 to 1.7). The quartet at $\delta$ 4.4 is the $\text{>CH}$ attached to electronegative O, deshielded into the 3.2 to 4.0 region and pushed a little higher by the adjacent $\text{C=O}$. The singlet at $\delta$ 5.0 fits $\text{ROH}$ ($\delta$ 0.5 to 6.0).

Work out splitting with n+1**
Splitting comes only from protons on the neighbouring carbon. The $\text{-CH}_3$ sees 1 proton on the $\text{CH}$, so n = 1 gives 1+1 = 2, a doublet. The $\text{>CH}$ sees 3 protons on the $\text{CH}_3$, so n = 3 gives 3+1 = 4, a quartet.

Explain why OH and COOH stay singlets**
The $\text{-OH}$ and $\text{-COOH}$ protons exchange rapidly and do not show coupling to neighbours under normal conditions, so each appears as a singlet with no splitting, even though they are near the $\text{CH}$ group.

Final answer: -COOH: $\delta$ 12.0, singlet
>CH: $\delta$ 4.4, quartet
-OH: $\delta$ 5.0, singlet
-CH3: $\delta$ 1.6, doublet

hints: Recall the inert standard added to every NMR sample that is defined as $\delta$ 0.0.
walkthrough:
Remember the zero point**
All $\delta$ values are measured relative to tetramethylsilane, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_4\text{Si}$, which is chosen because it gives a single sharp peak from 12 equivalent protons, is inert and volatile, and is set to $\delta$ 0.0.
Final answer: tetramethylsilane / TMS, $\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_4\text{Si}$

hints: Compare the formulas $\text{CDCl}_3$ and $\text{CHCl}_3$ and ask which one still contains $^1\text{H}$ nuclei that could absorb in proton NMR.
walkthrough:
Spot the interfering proton**
Proton NMR detects $^1\text{H}$ only. $\text{CHCl}_3$ has one $^1\text{H}$ that would absorb and hide sample peaks. Replacing H by D (deuterium, $^2\text{H}$) gives $\text{CDCl}_3$ which has no $^1\text{H}$ to absorb, leaving a clean spectrum while still dissolving the sample well.
Final answer: $\text{CDCl}_3$ contains no $^1\text{H}$ so gives no peak, whereas $\text{CHCl}_3$ contains $^1\text{H}$ which would give an extra absorption.

hints: Think about the journey of an injected sample through the column to the detector and what time interval is actually measured.
walkthrough:
Picture the column journey**
After injection the components travel at different speeds through the column. Retention time is simply the stopwatch time between putting the mixture in and the moment that particular component reaches the detector and its peak is recorded.
Final answer: Time taken from injection of the sample onto the column to detection / emergence of the component peak maximum.

hints: Recall that in gas liquid chromatography the moving phase must carry vapour without reacting and the fixed phase is a liquid coating that dissolves components differently.
walkthrough:
Match phases to GLC**
Gas liquid means gas moving, liquid fixed. An inert carrier gas such as $\text{He}$ or $\text{N}_2$ sweeps the vapour through without reacting. Inside the column a high boiling non-polar liquid coated on a solid absorbs and releases each component to different extents, causing separation.

Final answer: mobile phase: unreactive gas e.g. helium, nitrogen, argon
stationary phase: non-polar liquid e.g. oil, alkane coated on solid support

hints: Think about how the size of each peak relates to the amount of that component compared to the sum of all peaks.
walkthrough:
Use areas as amounts**
The detector response area is proportional to moles present. Measure or integrate the area of the lactic acid peak and the pentan-3-one peak, add them for total area, then: $$\text{% component} = \frac{\text{area of that peak}}{\text{total area}} \times 100\%$$ This gives the percentage composition of the mixture.
Final answer: Percentage = (area under peak for component / total area of all peaks) $\times$ 100%
